name: Documentary photography
summary: Photographs that bear witness to people, work and events. The maker gets close, earns trust and shows what the sitter needs the viewer to see.

philosophy.core_thesis: A photograph can be evidence and an appeal at once, if the maker stays honest about what happened and with whom.
design_principles: Use a 35mm or 50mm lens at 1 to 2.5m, so that the sitter, the room and the work share the frame.
Shoot in available light at ISO 400 to 1600, with a shutter of 1/60s or faster, and do not add flash.
Show the face and the hands, and the place that explains them.
Make 100 or more frames for one story, and edit down to 8 to 20 pictures.
Print with a full but natural range: no crushed blacks and no clipped skies.
Caption with who, where and when, in plain words.
anti_patterns: Staging a scene or rearranging people
Cropping out context that changes the meaning
Victim pose and pity as the only note

composition.framing: Medium and wide; the frame holds the person and the place that explains them.
composition.viewpoint: Eye height, handheld, 1 to 2.5m from the subject.
composition.geometry: Window frames, doorways and tools make the geometry; people sit inside layers of the room.
composition.subject_placement: Off centre with the eyes or the hands on a third line; context fills the rest.

principles.rule: Let 1 face or pair of hands take 25–40% of the frame, with the place around it.
Hold 3 planes: foreground object at 1m, person at 2m and room or street at 5m.
Put the eyes within 0.05 of the upper third line, at 0.33 of the height.
Use a door, window or tool to frame the person with a margin of 5–15%.
Keep informal balance: person on one side, work or object on the other, at a ratio of 0.7–1.4.

light.quality: Available light, as found: window light, overcast sky or a single lamp.
light.direction: From a window or door to the side; the face gets a soft modelling of 2:1 to 4:1.
light.time_of_day: Any; early and late light preferred

lens_and_camera.format: 35mm SLR or rangefinder; digital full frame as a modern equivalent
lens_and_camera.focus: Zone focus at 2m at f/8, or focus on the eyes at f/4.

colour_and_grade.treatment: Natural black and white with moderate grain, or true colour with no creative grade.
grade_recipe: Convert to monochrome with a neutral mix (R 40, G 50, B 10).
Set the black point at 2% and the white point at 97%.
Recover skies by −0.5 stop with a graduated filter; do not composite.
Add film grain, amount 15%, size 30%, as for Tri-X at ISO 400.
Crop by no more than 5%, and keep a caption with every frame.
colour_and_grade.grain: Tri-X 400: medium grain, visible at A4

subject_and_staging.staging: None. The maker spends days or weeks with the subject and photographs what happens.
subject_and_staging.direction: Ask for consent and for time; do not ask for a pose. Show the sitter the pictures when it is possible.

workflow: Make a contact sheet of every frame and mark the strongest.
Edit the series down to 8 to 20 pictures that run as a story.
Print in a natural range on grade 2 paper.
Write captions with name, place and date; check every fact.
post_processing.output: A photo essay of 8 to 20 pictures, with captions, in print, in a book or online.

canonical_works.work: Let Us Now Praise Famous Men

emotion.target_response: Engaged concern: the viewer sees a person, believes the scene and feels pulled toward it.

use_cases: image prompts for honest portraits at work
avoid_when: The brief needs a staged or glossy ideal.
The subjects have not agreed to be shown, or their safety is at risk.

modifiers.how: Go to a 28mm lens at f/8, zone-focus at 2.5m and wait for a gesture at 1/250s; keep strangers anonymous.
Move to a tripod and a 150mm lens at f/32, with even light and a frontal view; photograph the person as a type.

sources.title: Walker Evans and James Agee, Let Us Now Praise Famous Men (Houghton Mifflin, 1941)
Jorge Lewinski, The Naked Image: Photography Since 1945 (Macmillan, 1987)
